Rows 19 to 25 are retrospective: those logs reached earlier sessions that did not log them here, so any finding they drew is in the HANDOVER section of the build named; the facts in each row come from the log itself (tier as printed by the debrief plus the AI's raw numbers).*

**Project:** `StarTrek_TacticalCommand_GAME.html` — a single self-contained HTML5 file
(one `<script>`, one `<style>`, no external assets) implementing FASA *Starship Tactical
Combat Simulator* on a hex grid, plus an in-game Ship Recognition Database.

**Current deployed build: v2.18-S129.** (No build change since — a separate UI/UX
exploration happened after this, see the note below; it never touched this file.) Deployed at
`/mnt/user-data/outputs/StarTrek_TacticalCommand_GAME.html` (~9.2 MB, mostly embedded
ship-sprite/viewscreen-art PNGs as base64). There is currently only ONE game file — the
earlier `_temp_display_ver_NN` experimental track (ver_01 through ver_19) has been merged
into this mainline build and is now retired. If a future session finds any
`_temp_display_ver_NN` files still floating around, they are historical/superseded — this
file is ground truth.

Build discipline (never violate): one `<script>` + one real `<style>` tag; brace/paren/bracket
balance 0/0/0 in the extracted JS; validate with `check.js` (script/style tag counts + balance
+ `new Function()` syntax check) — **`node --check` on the extracted `<script>` body works
equally well and was used throughout §0.43-§0.65** if `check.js` isn't available in a given
session; NOT browser-testable in this environment (playtest externally — the user reports
back via combat logs and direct feedback); bump the version string in **all three** in-game
spots (`<title>`, `id="hdr-build"` header, and the startup `log(...)` line) plus this file and
README, on every build. **Next version → v2.19-Sxx.**

**A fourth place the version now effectively lives, as of §0.43-§0.53**: every build's
`log('BUILD vX.XX-SXXX -- ...', 'info')` call is itself a durable, in-file record of what
changed — not just a startup console message. When this document's own version tracking falls
behind (as it did for 15 builds leading into this entry), grep the game file for
`log('BUILD v` and read the missing entries out of it directly rather than treating that
history as lost. This does not replace writing it into HANDOVER properly — it's a recovery
path, not a substitute for keeping this file current.

**Escaping discipline (new, learned the hard way in §0.50 and §0.52)**: when inserting a new
`log('BUILD ...', 'info');` string via a text-editing tool (rather than typing it directly into
a code editor), a single backslash intended as a JS string escape (`\'`, `\u00a7`) is easy to
accidentally type as a literal double backslash (`\\'`, `\\u00a7`) depending on how the edit
tool handles its own input escaping. This produces a string that *looks* right when skimmed but
fails `node --check` with a cryptic "missing ) after argument list" pointing at the very end of
the string, not the actual mistake. If that specific error shows up right after adding a log
line, check for doubled backslashes first before looking anywhere else.

**Verification discipline that held up across a long session of ship-art work, keep doing
this**: never trust a search-and-replace or a "looks right" glance. When editing a specific
object (`SHIP_REGISTRY`, `SHIP_SPRITES`, `FRONT_VIEW_ART`, `CATALOG`) that shares key names
with another object in the same file, scope any find/replace to that object's own boundaries
first (`const OBJNAME = {...}` start/end), never a bare file-wide string search — a same-named
key living in two different objects (e.g. `D7RSM` exists in both `SHIP_SPRITES` and
`FRONT_VIEW_ART`) will silently edit the wrong one otherwise. After any image-embedding edit,
independently decode the base64 back out and visually view it — a passing `check.js` only
proves the file is syntactically valid, not that the right picture ended up in the right key.

### 0.1 — Why this handover was rewritten (documentation-gap incident, historical)

Earlier in this project's life, the game file advanced 22 builds while this HANDOVER and the
README were never updated, leaving both frozen on a stale version. Recovered by diffing the
actual file against the last known-good copy rather than trusting either party's memory.
**Standing lesson, still in force**: if this document's stated version ever doesn't match the
game file's actual `hdr-build` string, treat the game file as ground truth and re-diff from
scratch — don't assume the doc is merely "a little behind."

**A second instance of the same failure mode surfaced 2026-09-02**: the game code's "SHIP
EXPLOSIONS" section has referenced *"the full self-destruct/surrender design, see HANDOVER"*
since before this rewrite, but no such design existed anywhere in this file. It had to be
partially recovered from the user's own memory rather than any written record — see §3.2.
Design discussions that only exist as chat history are exactly as fragile as an unbumped
version number; write them down here the same session they happen, not "eventually."

### 0.2 — What changed in v1.55-S66 (playtest-feedback pass)

Four items from external playtesting. No image/sprite work this build, so none of the
base64/orientation discipline in §2.2 was exercised — but all of it still applies next time art
is touched.

1. **Boarding narrative** (`buildPowerKillNarrative()`, the `fates` object). The Klingon- and
   Romulan-winner capture paragraphs opened with "Warriors/Romulan officers crossed into the
   [X] hull" — flagged as awkward. All **six** affected entries (kli:fed, kli:kli, kli:rom,
   rom:fed, rom:kli, rom:rom) were reworded to varied boarding language ("boarding parties were
   aboard", "stormed aboard", "forced the ship's locks", "boarding officers came aboard",
   "boarded", "the boarding party came aboard"). Only the opening clause of each changed; the
   rest of every paragraph is untouched. Verified: zero "crossed into" strings remain.
2. **Federation cloak-readout fix** (`SENSOR_QUESTIONS`, Q2 "relative power allocation"). The
   readout unconditionally listed a `cloak` line item, so scanning a Federation ship reported a
   cloaking-power figure for a system it doesn't have. Now the cloak item is only pushed when
   `t.cloakCost > 0`. Federation (cloakCost 0) shows no cloak line; cloak-equipped Klingon/
   Romulan hulls are unaffected. This also correctly hides it for any other non-cloak hull.
3. **Per-phase tutorial coach** (new). A dismissible guidance card, keyed by phase family
   (power / tacadv / sensors / move / fire / repower), driven by `TUTORIAL_STEPS` and shown via
   `showTutorial(phase)` called at the end of `enterPhase()` — so it refreshes every phase and
   fires from game start (enterPhase('power') runs in the start callback). Header toggle
   `#hdr-tutorial` → `toggleTutorial()`; per-card dismiss `#tut-coach-x` → `dismissTutorialCard()`.
   **On by default.** State is an in-memory `let TUTORIAL_ON` — deliberately NOT localStorage,
   matching this file's existing no-storage convention (so the preference resets on reload).
4. **Firing-chart hit outlook** (new). `weaponHitOutlook(w)` reads `FIRING_CHARTS[w.chart]` at
   the current range (`hexDist(player,enemy)`) and returns the same success band the to-hit
   roll uses — `chart[range] = [min,max]`, hit on 1..max, so `max/10` IS the hit chance. Gates
   "OUT OF RNG" on BOTH `maxR<=0` AND `range > (w.maxRange||15)`, matching `fireWeapon()`'s real
   checks. Rendered as a colour-coded `.wpn-hit` badge injected into each weapon row in
   `initUI()` (which rebuilds rows every turn, so the estimate tracks the current range).
   Bands: VERY HIGH (9-10) / HIGH (7-8) / MODERATE (5-6) / LOW (3-4) / VERY LOW (1-2) / OUT.
   **Note:** it's a *pre-movement* estimate — power allocation precedes movement in the phase
   order, so range (and arc) can change before the shot. Labelled as such in-UI and in the
   tooltip. At the default start range of 15 hexes, every weapon correctly reads OUT OF RNG on
   turn 1 — not a bug; the ships genuinely start out of range and must close. Verified the band
   math against the real chart data with a standalone Node harness, not just by eye.

### 0.3 — What changed in v1.56-S67 (USS Constitution real ship art)

User supplied a fan reference sheet (`constitution_class_starship___high_resolution_01.jpg`,
1069×747) with five rendered views on one canvas: top-down (bow-left), profile, bottom-up
(all three sharing hull text reading "U.S.S. BRINDABELLA" / registry "NCC-1861"), plus a
3/4-front and 3/4-rear view (neither carries hull text). Request: use this as the USS
Constitution's real art, relettering the hull text to "U.S.S. CONSTITUTION" / "NCC-1700" in
matching font/size/color, embed what's usable immediately, shelve the rest for later.

**The near-miss this build almost caused, read this before touching sprite keys again:**
`SHIP_SPRITES.Constitution` and `FRONT_VIEW_ART` lookups are both keyed by each ship's
`spriteKey` field. The pre-existing `SHIP_SPRITES.Constitution` entry (a generic procedural
silhouette, not real art) is NOT specific to "USS Constitution" — grepping
`spriteKey:'Constitution'` turns up **four** SHIP_REGISTRY records: the top-level
`Constitution` record (which is actually **USS Enterprise, NCC-1701** — the registry's own
top-level key name is just an internal slug, not the ship's name) plus `Constitution_MkI`,
`Constitution_MkII`, `Constitution_MkIII` (all **USS Constitution, NCC-1700**, matching the
mark-naming-mismatch pattern already flagged for Chandley/D-7 in older notes). Overwriting
`SHIP_SPRITES.Constitution`/`FRONT_VIEW_ART.Constitution` with the new NCC-1700-lettered art
would have made Enterprise's tactical sprite and viewscreen incorrectly read "NCC-1700" too.
**Fix:** a brand-new key, `Constitution_NCC1700`, was added to both `SHIP_SPRITES` and
`FRONT_VIEW_ART`; only the three actual `Constitution_MkI/II/III` records were repointed to
it (`spriteKey:'Constitution_NCC1700'`). The Enterprise-owned `Constitution` key and its art
are completely untouched — Enterprise still uses the same generic silhouette + procedural
viewscreen fallback as before this build. **Any future work on Constitution-class ships must
grep every `spriteKey:'Constitution'` occurrence before assuming the key is free or ship-specific.**

**Relettering approach** (reusable for future hull-text edits): dark/light text pixels were
isolated via HSV-aware thresholding (plain grayscale threshold mis-fires on colored stripes —
learned the hard way on the profile view's red accent stripe, which is dark in luminance but
clearly not text), removed via either `cv2.inpaint` (works well on gradient-y/textured
surfaces like the saucer panel) or straight row/column-wise linear interpolation from clean
pixels just outside the text's bounding box (more reliable than inpainting on flat surfaces
with a hard color edge nearby, e.g. the profile stripe boundary or the bottom-up saucer's ring
pattern — inpainting kept leaving mottled residue there). New text was rendered in Liberation
Sans Bold (closest available system font to the source's bold sans hull lettering) sampled to
the original's exact dark-charcoal color. For the saucer's curved rim text specifically, a
reusable `draw_arc_text()` helper places each glyph by polar position (angle/radius from the
saucer's fitted circle center) with a *separate, dampened* rotation rate — position follows
the full angular sweep 1:1, but per-glyph rotation lags behind it (a `rot_scale` factor <1.0
on long strings). This was the key discovery: naive 1:1 tangent-following rotation
over-rotates the tail end of a long curved string well past what the source art actually
shows; the source's letters stay far more upright throughout the curve than a literal
"rotate to match the tangent" model predicts. Verified the arc math against real anchor
points hand-measured off the source image (not guessed), and separately verified letter
*order* with a rainbow-per-character debug render after an apparent "reversed spelling" turned
out to be tightly-overlapping rotated glyphs fooling the eye, not an actual ordering bug —
worth remembering before assuming a curved-text result is wrong from a blurry small-scale look.

**What's embedded now:**
- `SHIP_SPRITES.Constitution_NCC1700` — top-down tactical sprite. Extracted from the source's
  top-down view (which is bow-LEFT), background-removed, tightly cropped, rotated 90° to
  bow-UP, then scaled/centered on a 256×256 transparent canvas matching Reliant's exact fill
  ratio (67.1875% of canvas on the longest dimension) — verified against Reliant side-by-side.
- `FRONT_VIEW_ART.Constitution_NCC1700` — viewscreen portrait, from the source's 3/4-front
  view, background-removed, tightly cropped (native aspect ratio, no fixed canvas size,
  matching how Reliant/D10/Chandley/etc. are each their own native crop size).
- Both independently decoded back out of the saved game file and visually re-verified after
  insertion — not just eyeballed as PNGs before embedding. Neighboring entries
  (`SHIP_SPRITES.Constitution`/`D7`/`D7RSM`) were also re-decoded post-edit to confirm no
  collateral damage from the insert.

**What's shelved for later, not wired in:** `Constitution_integration.js` (new file, sits
alongside the main game file — NOT merged in) bundles the source sheet's profile, bottom-up,
and 3/4-rear views as base64 PNGs, same relettering treatment applied where those views
carried hull text (profile and bottom-up both did; rear did not). Follows the same "shelved
extra views" pattern already established in the Reliant/D-10 SHIP_SPRITES comments. To
integrate later: copy the relevant key(s) into `SHIP_SPRITES`/`FRONT_VIEW_ART` under a new,
deliberately-checked-for-collisions key — do not assume any name is free without grepping
`spriteKey:` first, per the near-miss above.

## 1. Full current feature set (consolidated, for a session with zero prior context)

- **Sound and weapon effects (as of v2.89-S200; details in §0.164 and wishlist C10)**: recorded or designed sounds for Federation phasers, lasers and torpedoes (launch and arming), Gorn beams and torpedoes, Romulan torpedoes, the older Klingon D-7 disruptors, plasma weapons (loading when armed; the "flame roar and spit" firing sound), ship destruction, Federation commit, proceed and bridge door, and six ambience recordings (setup; the bridge beds: Federation TOS, Federation TMP Enterprise, Klingon, Romulan; the Damage Control hum). Still generated: the Romulan, newer Klingon and Orion beams; the Klingon and Orion torpedoes; hit, shield and miss; move, phase, tactical, victory and defeat; the Gorn and Orion tactical bed, the Power tab hum (and pad, heard only by the Gorn and Orions now), and the Damage Control reactive layers. Torpedoes have six designed looks (Klingon Motion Picture, Federation x2, Romulan, Gorn, Orion); the older D-7s fire green bolts. The Power tab shows an "ARMED NOW" line and a weapon's name arms it.

- **Core FASA hex combat**: movement (facing, rotation cost, forward/reverse), three-phase
  turn structure (Sensors → Movement → Firing) × 3 sub-phases, tactical-advantage roll,
  power allocation (move/shields/weapons) with a two-step commit (Commit → ▶ Proceed to Combat
  / ↶ Revise Allocation; a zero-power commit warns explicitly instead of silently proceeding).
- **6 playable factions**: Federation, Klingon, Romulan, Gorn, Orion, plus Independent Merchants
  as a distinct viewing-instrument style in the viewscreen (see below) — 45 `SHIP_REGISTRY`

- **Cloaking**, **AI difficulty 1–5** with patrol-when-target-unseen logic, **optional house

  entries directly rather than trusting a remembered count, since that number changes whenever

- **NEW this update — Viewscreen**: the sidebar's Enemy Contact card no longer shows plain

  reusing the game's own `enemyTelemetryVisible()` and already-masked DOM telemetry text so it
  can never reveal more than the real HUD does. When no sensor lock is held: the portrait
  itself is genuinely blurred (`canvas.filter`), with a noise-scatter + pulsing dashed ring

  per-faction display styles — Federation (clean sans, rounded frame), Klingon (bold condensed,
  angular frame), Romulan (italic serif, elegant double-line frame), Orion (slanted, patched/

- **NEW this update — real ship art**: seven hulls have genuine bow-on viewscreen portraits

## 2. What's new in v1.54-S65 specifically (this merge)

Everything in §1 marked "NEW this update" was developed and iterated across a long series of
prior exchanges under a separate `_temp_display_ver_NN` filename track (ver_01 through ver_19),
deliberately kept out of the mainline file until proven out. That track is now merged and
retired. The full blow-by-blow development history (every mistake, every fix, every piece of
user feedback that shaped a decision) is NOT reproduced here — it served its purpose during
development. What's preserved below is only what remains actionable: open decisions, and
general lessons that will matter again the next time a ship gets real art.

### 2.1 — Open decisions (not resolved by merging — still genuinely open)

- **Chandley's livery**: two variants exist on the source sheet (Livery A — grey/orange,
  registry NCC-2301; Livery B — grey/blue accent). Livery A is what's currently wired into
  `FRONT_VIEW_ART.ChandleyClass`, chosen unilaterally (first-listed on the sheet, muted tone
  closer to the existing live sprite) — **not a user confirmation**. Swap to B on request; see
  `Chandley_integration.js` for both.
- **Mark-naming mismatches against the FASA source**: the live registry's `Chandley_MkI/II/III`
  doesn't map cleanly onto the FASA source's Mk I/III/IV for that hull (no Mk II in the source
  table at all). Not resolved, not blocking — just don't assume the live naming is FASA-literal
  for this ship if it matters later.
- **D-10 crimson/gunmetal liveries**: confirmed to be earmarked for a rogue/pirate Klingon
  vessel, not this ship's alternate paint — but no art for either has actually been supplied
  yet.
- **Most of the 45-hull roster still has no real front-on art** — as of v1.56-S67 that's eight
  ships (the seven from §1, plus USS Constitution NCC-1700 via the new `Constitution_NCC1700`
  key — see §0.3). Everything else still correctly uses the procedural fallback, including
  Enterprise's `Constitution`-keyed sprite, which remains generic/silhouette despite the
  confusingly-similar key name (see §0.3's near-miss writeup). This came up once already as a
  user memory mismatch (assuming Constitution had real art before it did) — worth
  double-checking `FRONT_VIEW_ART`'s actual key list directly before assuming any specific
  ship has real art.

### 2.2 — General lessons (apply to any future ship art work, not specific to one ship)

- **A tight, alpha-cropped extraction is right for `FRONT_VIEW_ART` as-is, but WRONG for
  `SHIP_SPRITES` without repadding first.** `drawShipSprite()` stretches the *entire* source
  canvas — ship plus whatever padding surrounds it — into a fixed square box sized to the hex.
  Every correctly-sized existing sprite has the ship filling only ~27–69% of its 256×256
  canvas, never close to 100%. Before dropping any new tight crop into `SHIP_SPRITES`: resize
  it so its longest dimension fills ~67% of a new 256×256 transparent canvas, centered.
- **Sprites must be "nose-up"** — `drawShipSprite()`'s own code comment says so, and every
  working sprite (check `Reliant` as the reference) has the bow at the top, aft at the bottom.
  A source reference sheet's own stated orientation (which way the artist happened to draw a
  particular view) is not evidence of which way is "up" for this game's convention — rotate
  as needed and verify against a known-good sprite's layout, not by any other proxy.
- **Text reading right-side-up after a rotation is NOT evidence the ship orientation is
  correct.** These are unrelated properties — a label can read correctly while the ship is
  drawn upside-down relative to convention. Verify orientation by checking which structural
  element is where (saucer/bow vs. nacelles/aft), never by text legibility.
- **A reference sheet's layout (which row is "front," which is "bottom," etc.) is not
  transferable between sheets.** One artist's convention ("bottom row = front view") does not
  generalize to the next sheet. If the user hasn't stated a sheet's layout explicitly, don't
  infer one angle's identity from another sheet's pattern — ask, or verify structurally (does
  this view show a forward-facing deflector/sensor face, or does it look like it's looking up
  at a belly/equipment rack).
- **When a small unrelated element (an artist's avatar, a watermark, a logo) overlaps the
  region being extracted**: `scipy.ndimage.label` connected-component analysis reliably
  separates a genuine ship silhouette from unrelated small blobs by pixel-count alone (ship
  bodies have consistently been 5–15× larger than any contaminating element across every sheet
  processed this session) — far more reliable than eyeballing a bounding box.
- **(2026-09-23, K-23) Removing a painted element that straddles structural seams: do NOT trust
  generic inpainting.** OpenCV Telea and Navier-Stokes both pulled background grey into the hull's
  bottom edge and left a visible notch, because the glow mask (dot + dilated red halo) reached the
  edge line. What worked: profile the rows' luminance around the mask to find the structural bands
  (lit panel face / seam / dark lower band / hull edge / background), then fill each band with its
  own rule — vertical MIRROR of the unmasked rows just above for the lit face (keeps real metal
  texture), horizontal interpolation between unmasked neighbours for the seam, dark band and edge
  rows (+ tiny noise on flat dark bands), then a 0.7px feather on the filled pixels only. Judge
  at native display size, not only zoomed.
- **(2026-09-25, Bright One) `view` never reaches the user — only `present_files` on a copy in
  `/mnt/user-data/outputs/` does.** Two full rounds of proof/rejection happened because this session
  showed visual proof only via `view`. The user twice said "garbage" while actually reacting to
  seeing nothing at all the first time. ANY visual proof meant for the user's eyes needs the explicit
  outputs-copy + present_files step, every time.
- **(2026-09-25, Bright One) Fused/overlapping source art: verify a "removable artifact" is really
  removable before cutting it.** What first looked like debris turned out to be part of the ship's
  own real geometry, damaged by an earlier cut — confirmed by checking for a matching feature
  elsewhere on the model before assuming pixels are junk. When a user rejects a fix with no detail,
  ask them to point at the exact spot rather than re-guessing blind.
- **(2026-09-24, Larson) Check for a REAL alpha channel before colour-keying.** This sheet's background
  was already transparent (mode RGBA, real per-pixel alpha), not a solid colour — running the grey/black
  keying recipe's closing step anyway added a false halo that merged two side-by-side views into one
  bounding box. Test `im.mode` and whether alpha actually varies BEFORE choosing an extraction method.
- **(2026-09-24, Andor) Black-background sheets:** luminance-band alpha un-premultiplied against black; fill only small
  enclosed holes, keep large enclosed gaps transparent; select views by connected component, never by overlapping
  crop rectangles (details §0.77).
- **(2026-09-23, v2.20-S131) "Detached from the main hull" ≠ debris.** A connected-component scan
  of all viewscreen art flagged thousands of detached pixels; a magenta-overlay visual check showed
  nearly all were real parts separated by transparent gaps (wingtip pods, antenna masts, running
  lights). Only margin-pinned blobs far from the hull were genuine debris. Always LOOK before
  deleting pixels.
- **(2026-09-23, K-23) Grey-metal hull on a grey sheet background:** a colour-distance key alone
  would punch holes in highlight panels that match the backdrop. Use the filled connected-component
  silhouette as a solid core (alpha 1 after a 1px erosion), soft alpha only in a ~4px edge band
  from colour distance, then defringe that band by un-mixing the known background colour
  (`rgb = (obs - (1-α)·bg) / α`). No halo on dark backgrounds; engine glow plumes survive.

### 0.4 — What changed in v1.57-S68 (endgame redesign — panel + synced explosion shockwave)

Long-running design conversation, worked through entirely as interactive mockups before any
code was touched (search this session's history for the widget iterations if the reasoning
behind a choice below isn't obvious from the code alone).

**The full-screen `#victory-screen` overlay is gone, fully removed** (HTML, CSS, and the old
`showVictoryOverlay()` — search for it if a stale reference ever reappears; it shouldn't).
Replaced by `#eg-panel`, nested *inside* `#tac-log-panel` (not a sibling — this matters because
the log panel is user-resizable via `#tac-log-resize`, so the new panel needs to inherit
whatever width the player has dragged it to, not a hardcoded value). The panel slides up from
the bottom of the log column only. **The tactical map is never covered** — this was the entire
point of the redesign: previously the map (and any explosion playing on it) vanished under an
opaque full-screen div almost immediately after a kill.

Panel contents: title (VICTORY/DEFEAT/MUTUAL DESTRUCTION, color-coded), a narrative that starts
collapsed to ~2 lines with a "Read full narrative" toggle (`toggleEgNarrative()`) that expands
in place via `max-height` transition rather than growing the whole panel taller, a "Download
combat log" link (reuses the existing `exportCombatLog()`), turn/shot stats, and a "New
Mission" button (reuses the existing `location.reload()` — no new reset logic needed). Decided
against a separate "Close/Exit" action after discussion — New Mission is the only way out,
matching how the old overlay worked, just relocated.

**Ship destruction (`playDestructionSequence()`) was substantially rebuilt**, not just
restyled. All three of these effects are driven by one shared `progress` value (0→1 over a
fixed `EXPAND_MS`), specifically because an earlier version had the fireball and the shockwave
running on separate, unsynchronized timings and it visibly showed — the fireball would finish
its whole burst-and-fade cycle while the shockwave was still crawling outward, reading as two
uncoordinated animations rather than one explosion:
1. A brief white flash + soft radial glow at the instant of detonation (`t < 350ms`), for
   impact — this is pure visual flavor, not derived from any rule.
2. The fireball itself (the real `EXPLOSION_FRAMES` chit art, already in the codebase — no new
   art was added) now **grows in size** as `progress` advances instead of staying fixed, and
   fades out right at the end of the timeline instead of finishing early and just sitting there.
   Drawn with `globalCompositeOperation='lighter'` (canvas equivalent of the CSS
   `lighten`/`screen` blend tried in mockups) so it glows against the dark map instead of
   looking flat.
3. **A hex-accurate shockwave, reusing the FASA blast-damage rule for real** (see
   `calculateExplosionDamage`'s range-10 falloff and the "Damage From Explosions" rulebook
   table already cited there) — for every hex within that true 10-hex reach, computed with the
   game's own `hexDist`/`hexCen` (not reimplemented — directly reused), **only that hex's single
   edge facing away from the blast origin** flashes as the wavefront passes over it. No fill,
   no filled ring, no lingering trail — arrived at after several rounds of the user rejecting
   progressively closer attempts (a filled disk, then a full-hexagon-outline ring, before
   landing on single-edge-only). The edge segments are precomputed once per explosion (a few
   hundred hexes at most on the real 24×18 board — cheap), not recomputed every animation frame.

**A real bug was fixed as a direct side effect of touching this code, not a separate ask:**
`checkVictory()`'s win-determination previously had no branch for both hulls reaching zero
superstructure in the same resolution (a `pd && ed` mutual-destruction case, which the code
already explicitly anticipated for the *explosion-sequencing* — it already played both ships'
destruction animations in that case — but the win/lose *label* logic didn't match). It silently
fell through to declaring the player the loser. Now shows "MUTUAL DESTRUCTION" and narrates
both sides via `buildKillNarrative()` called twice. This can already happen from ordinary
simultaneous combat resolution today — it does not require `applyExplosionDamage` (§3.2) to be
wired up. That dead code was deliberately left untouched; only the display bug was fixed.

**Still open, not addressed this build:**
- Whether stray clicks on the now-visible-and-clickable map during the endgame sequence need
  guarding against (the map is inert once `GS.over=true`, but worth a pass to confirm nothing
  in existing map click-handlers fires when the game is over).
- Whether `#combat-log` should have pointer-events disabled while `#eg-panel` covers its bottom
  portion (currently harmless either way — the log is covered, not interactive underneath, but
  its scroll listener isn't explicitly suppressed).
- The fuller surrender/self-destruct design (§3.2, now with a detailed Gorn/Orion disposition
  matrix — see that section) remains untouched, on the backlog. (Admiral AI tuning, also
  flagged in this section previously, was fixed the same session — see §0.5.)

### 0.5 — What changed in v1.58-S69 (Admiral-tier AI tuning — fixes §3.1)

All three weaknesses diagnosed in §3.1 from the user's combat log were implemented and
independently verified this build, not just described:

1. **`aiAllocatePower()`'s `D===5` branch now reads its own hull, not just the player's.** Added
   `ownHullPct = s.superstructure/s.superstructureMax` alongside the existing (player) `hullPct`.
   New branch: when `ownHullPct<0.35 && hullPct>=0.4` (badly hurt, enemy isn't), shifts to a
   defensive split (`shields=Math.floor(tot*0.55)`, more move, weapons only get what's left)
   instead of continuing the same offense-oriented split it used at full health. Verified with a
   standalone Node harness against several scenarios (healthy ship, critically hurt ship, and a
   mutual slugfest where both sides are hurt) — confirmed the healthy case is byte-for-byte
   identical to the old formula (no regression) and the mutual-slugfest case correctly stays
   aggressive rather than overcorrecting into passivity just because the AI itself is also hurt.
2. **Weapon power is now capped via `Math.min(weapPwr, armable)`** on every branch of `D===5`,
   where `armable = s.weapons.filter(w=>w.alive).reduce((a,w)=>a+w.maxPower,0)` — the same
   pattern `D===1` (Cadet) already used. Any power the cap removes from weapons flows to shields
   automatically, since shields is computed as `tot-move-weapPwr` (or vice versa) after the cap
   is applied, not before.
3. **`aiDoMove()`'s `tryMove()` "optimal range" branch now checks weapon-arc coverage for
   `D===5` specifically**, not just distance. Before turning toward the pure-distance heading
   `wf`, it checks whether the CURRENT facing already keeps at least one alive weapon's arc on
   the tracked target (reusing the existing `weaponArcCoversTarget()` — not reimplemented). If
   not, it searches all 6 facings for the one that covers the most alive weapons and steers
   toward that instead of `wf`. Falls back to the original distance-only `wf` behavior whenever
   `D!==5`, no weapons are alive, or the current facing already has coverage — so this is
   additive, not a rewrite of the movement logic for other difficulty tiers. Deliberately scoped
   to only the "optimal range" branch (where the diagnosed bug actually manifested), not the
   close-in/back-off branches, and deliberately NOT applied to `D===6` (Legend), which is
   hand-authored from real combat logs and shouldn't have its movement logic altered by a fix
   aimed at a different tier.

**Not touched, and shouldn't be inferred as related:** `D===6` (Legend)'s own formulas, the
surrender/self-destruct design (§3.2), and the still-dead `applyExplosionDamage` (also §3.2).

### 0.6 — What changed in v1.59-S70 (destroyed ships stayed visible after exploding — real bug,
fixed; plus a difficulty-mislabeling correction on the log that found it)

**Source:** user-submitted combat log, `combat_log_2026-09-03-21-59-22.txt` (v1.58-S69) —
player-controlled Orion `Wanderer` vs. enemy Klingon `IKV Stronger Bird` (D-32). User reported
watching the enemy ship's explosion play (including what looked like the shockwave visually
reaching their own ship), but the destroyed Klingon hull remained fully visible on the map
afterward — "it needs to be removed if it blew up."

**The bug, traced to actual code, not just the symptom:** `renderTac()`'s ship-drawing loop
(`[GS.player,GS.enemy].forEach(s=>{...})`, search for that exact line) had no check anywhere
for `s.superstructure<=0`. Its only special case was for an undetected cloaked enemy (draws a
"CONTACT LOST" ghost instead of the hull). A destroyed ship fell through to the normal draw
path — full hull sprite, shield rings, glow — every single time. Since `playDestructionSequence()`
calls `renderTac()` on every animation frame to refresh the background before layering the
flash/fireball/shockwave on top (see §0.4), the "destroyed" ship was being drawn completely
normally underneath its own explosion for the entire sequence. Once the explosion finished
fading, nothing was left to indicate anything had happened — the ship was still sitting there,
fully intact-looking. **Fix:** added `if(s.superstructure<=0) return;` as the first line inside
that forEach, before even the cloak check. A ship now disappears from the map the instant its
explosion sequence begins, for either side (this is symmetric — the player's own ship is
equally affected if it's the one destroyed). Deliberately scoped to actual hull destruction
only — the separate power-loss/"adrift"/surrender ending does NOT zero out `superstructure`, so
a ship that goes dead-in-space from a power loss (rather than exploding) is correctly
unaffected and remains visible, matching that it didn't actually blow up.

**A second, separate finding from the same log, unrelated to the rendering bug:** the user
asked to keep this log "as an example for Admiral difficulty — orions," but the numbers say
otherwise. The AI's logged allocation (`Move 8→2pts, Shields 10→20pts, Weapons 22`, `tot=40`)
is an *exact* match for `D===2` (Ensign)'s hardcoded formula — `move=8; shields=10;
weapPwr=tot-move-shields` — not anything the `D===5` (Admiral) branch can produce (verified by
hand-computing all three Admiral sub-branches against the same `tot=40` and confirming none of
them land on shields=10/weapons=22; only Ensign's fixed constants do, and exactly). **This
match was very likely played at Ensign difficulty, not Admiral** — flagging this clearly so the
log isn't mistaken for an Admiral-tier reference point later (e.g. if someone revisits §3.1's
Admiral tuning and goes looking for more example logs). If the user intended to select Admiral
and it didn't take, that's worth them checking on their end; nothing in this session's tracing
suggests a bug in difficulty *selection* itself, only that this specific log's AI behavior
matches Ensign's known formula precisely.

**Housekeeping note for future changelog edits:** this build's own startup `log(...)` string
had a double-escaped-apostrophe bug (`\\'` instead of `\'`) introduced during editing, caught by
`check.js` before shipping and fixed — the second time this exact mistake has happened in this
project's history (see v1.57-S68's changelog for the first). Worth double-checking apostrophe
escaping specifically, not just running `check.js` and trusting a single PASS was inevitable.

### 0.7 — What changed in v1.60-S71 (real art for three Klingon Bird-of-Prey-hull ships)

**Source:** user-supplied reference sheet (`bird_of_prey_Klingon_01.jpg`, 827×992), six rendered
views of a single Klingon Bird-of-Prey-shaped hull design: top-down, bottom (ventral), a unique
3/4 above-and-forward angle, profile, 3/4-rear/aft, and front. No hull text or registry markings
anywhere on this ship — unlike every prior ship-art pass, no relettering was needed at all.

**The actual request, once clarified — read this before assuming "one ship, one art pass"
like prior sessions:** this single reference sheet was meant to represent **three different
named ships already in `SHIP_REGISTRY`** that share one hull design at three size classes, not
one ship. Confirmed directly with the user after an initial miscommunication (they'd said "save
for later" the first time these images came up, then clarified a turn later that they wanted it
wired in and interpreted as three ships, not one) — this is worth remembering as a pattern: when
a user describes an asset in terms of multiple in-game entities before uploading only one image,
check which entities already exist and what their established sizing/roles are, rather than
assuming a 1:1 image-to-ship mapping.

The three ships, confirmed via `spriteKey`, each used by exactly one `SHIP_REGISTRY` entry (no
sharing, no collision risk — checked before touching anything, this project has been burned by
assuming a key was free before):
- `K22BirdOfPrey` — IKV Bird of Prey (K-22, Class V), small scout, "about a dozen officers and
  men" per the user.
- `D32StrongerBird` — IKV Stronger Bird (D-32, Class VII), the mid-size cruiser from the
  `combat_log_2026-09-03-21-59-22.txt` fight referenced in §0.6.
- `L42GreatBird` — IKV Great Bird (L-42, Class IX-X), the frigate, meant to fill essentially the
  entire hex.

**Sizing methodology:** rather than inventing new fill ratios, measured the THREE EXISTING
procedural-placeholder sprites' actual fill percentage of the 256×256 canvas (bbox of longest
dimension ÷ 256) before replacing anything: `K22BirdOfPrey` ≈19.5%, `D32StrongerBird` ≈52.7%,
`L42GreatBird` ≈99.6%. The same master top-down artwork (rotated bow-up from the source's
bow-left orientation, verified visually) was then scaled to match each of those three existing
ratios exactly, so **relative ship size on the tactical map is unchanged from before this
build** — only the art itself changed, from procedural silhouette to the real reference art.

**What's now live:**
- `SHIP_SPRITES.K22BirdOfPrey`, `SHIP_SPRITES.D32StrongerBird`, `SHIP_SPRITES.L42GreatBird` —
  all three replaced in place (same keys, no `SHIP_REGISTRY` changes needed since there was no
  key-sharing to work around this time, unlike the Constitution/Enterprise near-miss).
- Three brand-new `FRONT_VIEW_ART` entries (none of these three ships had any real viewscreen
  art before this build — all fell back to the procedural viewscreen render). **All three use
  the identical front-view crop** — this angle is not scaled per hull size the way the tactical
  sprite is, since `FRONT_VIEW_ART` has no established per-ship-size scaling convention (it's
  always been tight native-aspect-ratio crops with wildly different sizes already, e.g. D10 at
  360×80 vs. Loknar at 519×268). If distinguishing the three ships' viewscreen portraits by
  apparent size ever matters, that would be new work, not something this build did.
- Both independently re-decoded from the actual saved game file (not the working PNGs) and
  visually re-verified after insertion, plus a spot-check on unrelated neighboring sprites
  (`Reliant`, `D7`) to confirm no collateral damage from the edit.

**Relationship to `D32StrongerBird_integration.js` (the reserve file from the previous, pre-
clarification turn):** that file's `topdown_sprite` and `front` payloads are now duplicated
live in the game via the above. The file itself was NOT deleted or modified — its other four
views (`bottomview`, `unique34`, `profile`, `rearaft`) are still reserve-only, not used by any
in-game system. See the updated §5 entry for that file.

### 0.8 — What changed in v1.61-S72 (fixed two real problems in the v1.60-S71 Klingon art)

**Both found from the user actually playing the build, not from anything caught in review —
worth remembering that "check.js passes and it decodes to the right picture" is necessary but
not sufficient; the art can still be wrong in ways that only show up on the actual hex grid.**

**Problem 1 — background removal was eating the ship's own dark detail, not just the
background.** The transparency step used a flat rule: any pixel darker than a brightness
threshold becomes transparent. This works fine for a pure black backdrop, but this ship's
forward gun booms are ALSO dark-colored (a weapon barrel, not background) — so parts of them
were being silently erased, which read as "clipped" wing guns even though the crop boundary
itself was fine (verified this directly: the crop already included the full gun boom region;
the pixels were being removed by the transparency step afterward, not left out of the crop).
**Fix:** switched to flood-fill transparency — label connected dark regions, and only make
transparent the ones that actually touch the image border (i.e., are provably connected to the
real background), leaving any dark region enclosed by non-dark pixels (like a dark gun barrel
surrounded by the ship's own hull) fully opaque regardless of how dark it is. Reprocessed all
six extracted views with this method, not just the tactical sprite that showed the problem.
**If a future ship-art pass hits a similarly dark-detailed hull (black hull plating, shadowed
recesses, dark weapon mounts), use flood-fill transparency from the start, not a flat threshold.**

**Problem 2 — `L42GreatBird` was scaled past the hex's actual boundary, not just "large."**
§0.7 sized this ship to match its *old* placeholder's fill ratio, measured as 99.6% of the
256×256 sprite canvas's longest dimension. That measurement was against the wrong reference
frame. The actual in-game hex, as drawn by `hpath()` (search for it — vertices at `60*i - 30`
degrees for `i` in 0..5), has flat sides on the left and right and points at top and bottom:
point-to-point height = `2r`, flat-to-flat width = `1.732r` (`sqrt(3)*r`). Since
`drawShipSprite()` stretches the full 256×256 canvas into a square exactly `2r` tall (matching
the hex's own height), **a ship's content must stay under `1.732/2 = 86.6%` of the canvas
WIDTH to avoid poking past the hex's flat left/right edges** — regardless of how tall it is,
since height alone was never the binding constraint here. Confirmed by direct calculation
(`sqrt(3)/2 = 0.8660254...`), not approximated. `L42GreatBird` at 99.6% width blew well past
that 86.6% ceiling; the other two ships (`D32StrongerBird` at 52.7%, `K22BirdOfPrey` at 19.5%)
were already comfortably under it and needed no change. **Fix:** rescaled `L42GreatBird` to
82% width — still dramatically the largest of the three, genuinely reading as "fills the hex,"
but with real margin under the 86.6% ceiling rather than exceeding it. Verified all three
sprites' actual embedded widths against this 86.6% figure with a standalone calculation after
re-decoding them from the saved game file, not by eye.

**Takeaway worth keeping for any future sprite work, not just this ship:** the 256×256 canvas's
width and height are NOT equally "safe" — the canvas height maps directly to the hex's true
height, but the canvas width has an effective ceiling of ~86.6%, not 100%, before content
starts overflowing the hex's flat sides. `Reliant`'s known-good 67.2% width has always been
comfortably under this ceiling, which is presumably why it was never flagged before — this
project got lucky that no prior sprite happened to test the actual limit until this one did.

### 0.9 — What changed in v1.62-S73 (Klingon top-down art replaced again — asymmetric wingtip
booms traced to the source reference sheet itself, not a processing bug)

**The user reported a second problem after v1.61-S72**: a "green gun boom from another image
of the ship from another angle," visible on the starboard wingtip specifically. This turned out
to be real, but not for the reason initially assumed.

**What the investigation found, in order:** Decoded the live sprite in isolation — clean, no
stray fragments floating separately from the ship. Zoomed the starboard and port wingtips at
matching scale and found a genuine, unambiguous asymmetry: **port had one gun boom, starboard
had two.** Coordinate-math attempts to trace the extra boom's exact pixel origin back through
the crop→rotate→scale chain accumulated too much estimation error to be conclusive on their
own. What settled it: tracing both wingtips directly on the **original uploaded reference
sheet** (not any processed intermediate), with wide, unambiguous crops confirmed clear of any
other sheet content nearby. Both traces held up — **the source art itself draws two booms on
one wingtip and one on the other.** This was not bleed from the adjacent bottom-view image
(that was checked and ruled out specifically), not a crop-boundary error, and not something
introduced by the flood-fill transparency fix in v1.61-S72. It was simply how the reference
sheet was drawn.

**Since this was a genuine source-asymmetry, not a bug, the honest move was to ask the user
how they wanted it handled** (symmetric one-boom, symmetric two-boom, or leave the asymmetry as
authentic to the source) rather than silently pick one. **The user resolved it directly** by
re-cropping their own reference image and supplying a new, tighter top-down view by hand,
explicitly confirmed clean — both wingtips show exactly one boom each in the new source.

**What changed:** the new user-supplied crop became the master top-down source for all three
ships, reprocessed with the exact same pipeline established in v1.61-S72 (flood-fill
transparency from the image border, then scaled to the same three safe hex-width ratios: 19.5%
/ 52.7% / 82%). Front-view art (`FRONT_VIEW_ART`) was NOT touched this round — only
`SHIP_SPRITES.K22BirdOfPrey` / `D32StrongerBird` / `L42GreatBird` were replaced, since the
front-view crop was never implicated in the wingtip asymmetry. Verified: both wingtips now show
exactly one boom each, confirmed by decoding the sprite straight out of the saved game file
(not the working PNGs) and viewing it at 3× zoom with no interpolation blur.

**Process lesson for future ship-art work:** flood-fill transparency (v1.61-S72's fix) only
solves *dark* contamination connected to the image border — it does nothing for *colored*
bleed from an adjacent reference-sheet panel, since colored content never looks like
"background" to a brightness-based method regardless of connectivity. When a symmetric part
(wingtips, nacelles, weapon mounts) looks asymmetric after extraction, checking left vs. right
at matching zoom and scale is a fast, reliable diagnostic — and if an asymmetry traces all the
way back to the original source file itself, that's a genuine content question for the user to
resolve, not something to keep guessing at through pixel analysis alone.

### 0.10 — What changed in v1.63-S74 (Klingon front-view/viewscreen art replaced — clipped
starboard gun rail, same category of issue as §0.9, resolved the same way)

**The user found a second clipping problem after v1.62-S73**, this time in `FRONT_VIEW_ART`
rather than `SHIP_SPRITES`: the starboard gun rail was cut off in the viewscreen portrait.
Rather than repeat the multi-round diagnosis from §0.9, **the user supplied a clean,
pre-verified replacement image directly** — explicitly to avoid another back-and-forth. Before
processing it, both sides were checked for symmetry at matching zoom (learned from §0.9 not to
assume a supplied image is automatically correct just because it's new) — confirmed clean, both
gun rails intact and matching, with a claw-like tip at each end.

Processed with the same flood-fill transparency method as §0.9 (verified the resulting tight
bbox crop — height dropped from 73px to 41px — was trimming genuine black margin, not eating
content, by independently re-measuring the original image's own brightness-threshold bbox and
confirming it matched). Wired into all three ships' `FRONT_VIEW_ART` entries
(`K22BirdOfPrey`/`D32StrongerBird`/`L42GreatBird`, which have always shared one identical
crop — this hasn't changed). **`SHIP_SPRITES` (the top-down tactical icons) were not touched
this build** — only the viewscreen art. Verified by decoding all three `FRONT_VIEW_ART` entries
straight out of the saved game file (confirmed byte-identical to each other, as expected for a
shared crop) and spot-checking `SHIP_SPRITES.D32StrongerBird` and `Reliant` to confirm neither
was disturbed by an edit that should have been scoped to a completely different object.

### 0.11 — What changed in v1.64-S75 (kill narrative now reflects the full volley, not just the
killing weapon)

**Source:** user-submitted combat log, `combat_log_2026-09-04-10-46-28.txt` (v1.63-S74) — USS
Constitution vs. IKV Bird of Prey (K-22). The user pointed out that the end-of-game narrative
said "a single photon torpedo" delivered the kill, when the actual exchange fired two torpedo
tubes (`FP-1 Tube 1` and `Tube 2`) in the same `FIRE ALL`. Their framing, worth keeping exactly:
*"If an attacking ship opens up with everything and destroys a ship, that tells a different
story than it using one single torpedo."*

**Confirmed in the actual code, not assumed:** `buildKillNarrative()` had `isTorpedo ? "a
single photon torpedo" : ...` hardcoded — the word "single" was unconditional, regardless of
how many weapons actually fired alongside the one that landed the kill. `GS.killBlow` (set at
the moment a hit would bring superstructure to ≤0) only ever recorded the ONE weapon involved
in that specific hit, with no concept of "how many others fired in the same exchange."

**The fix required more care than a simple counter, because of how weapons actually fire.**
Both the player's `fireAllWeapons()`/`fireWeapon()` and the AI's `resolveShipFiring()` stagger
multi-weapon volleys 130ms apart via `setTimeout`, so a kill can land on an EARLY weapon in a
volley while later ones are still queued, unresolved. **Traced this exact case in the user's
own log**: the killing round was `FIRE ALL: 2 weapons firing` — Tube 1 hit and killed
(superstructure to 0), Tube 2 fired 130ms later and missed. A naive "count each shot as it
resolves" counter would have shown 1 at the moment of the kill (Tube 2 not yet resolved),
*still* undercounting — which would not have actually fixed the user's complaint. **The real
fix**: commit the full intended batch size to a per-ship `_volleyCount` up front, the instant
`fireAllWeapons()` (or the AI's equivalent) computes how many weapons are about to fire — not
incrementally as each one resolves. Verified against the exact user scenario with a standalone
Node simulation (not just read the code and assumed it worked): confirmed `totalWeaponsThisVolley`
reads `2` at the moment of the kill, matching the real log precisely.

**Mechanics, for anyone touching this again:**
- `s._volleyCount` resets to `0` in `endTurn()`, alongside the existing `w.fired=false` reset
  (same granularity: per-turn, not per-sub-phase, since a weapon that fires in sub-phase 1
  can't fire again in sub-phase 2 or 3 of the same turn anyway).
- `fireAllWeapons()` adds `ready.length` to `GS.player._volleyCount` immediately, before the
  staggered loop starts, then calls `fireWeapon(w.id, true)` for each — the second argument
  (`countedInBatch`) tells `fireWeapon()` not to increment again for these calls.
- A standalone individual weapon click (bypassing FIRE ALL) calls `fireWeapon(wid)` with no
  second argument, so it increments by 1 itself — correct for a genuinely standalone shot.
- The AI's `resolveShipFiring()` does the equivalent: `shooter._volleyCount += weapons.length`
  once, before its own staggered `forEach`, with no further per-weapon increment inside it.
- `GS.killBlow` now carries `totalWeaponsThisVolley`, read by `buildKillNarrative()`: 1 weapon
  keeps the original "a single X" phrasing; 2 becomes "a pair of shots"; 3+ becomes "opened up
  with everything she had — N weapons fired in the same exchange."

**Known limitation, small and honestly disclosed rather than silently accepted:** the AI's
`weapons` count in `resolveShipFiring()` is taken before the per-weapon arc check runs, so if
one of those weapons turns out to be out-of-arc when its turn comes up in the stagger, it still
counted toward the volley total even though it never actually fired a shot. This is a narrative
flavor detail, not a mechanical one, and fixing it properly would mean restructuring the arc
check to run before counting — judged not worth the complexity for a text-flavor number. If
this ever matters more than it does now, that's where to start.

**Two more things raised in the same message, logged but not acted on this build:**
- **The difficulty slider defaults to Ensign (`value="2"`) every time**, and since "New
  Mission" is a full `location.reload()`, it resets on every single game — it does not
  remember a previous session's choice. This is very likely why three combat logs submitted in
  a row (this one included) all matched Ensign's exact hardcoded power-allocation formula
  despite being described as Admiral-difficulty examples — the slider needs to be manually
  moved before every match, not just once. Not treating this as a bug to fix (the UI does
  clearly show "ENSIGN" both on the setup screen and in the header — it's not hidden), but
  flagging it here since it's now caused confusion three times in a row. If Admiral-specific
  logs are wanted going forward, double-check the slider position before launching.
- **"Bird of Preys work better in a group" / multi-ship combat** — the user's own observation
  from this fight (`IKV Bird of Prey` folded fast to a Constitution) plus an explicitly stated
  future idea: *"multiple ship combat is a later thing I have in my head."* Logged here as a
  named future direction, not scoped or designed at all yet — no ruleset research done, no
  implementation approach considered. Whoever picks this up should start from scratch on
  design, the same way §3.3's Advanced ruleset tier did, not assume anything here beyond "the
  user wants this eventually."

**CORRECTION, one turn later — the "difficulty tier to learn from the user's play" note above
was wrong.** The user clarified: it's not about which difficulty happened to be selected in a
given log at all — **`D===6` Legend is specifically the tier meant to learn from the user's own
demonstrated tactics**, regardless of what difficulty a submitted log's AI opponent was playing
at. This actually already matches how Legend's code is structured and commented ("hand-authored
from the user's own combat logs") — this session's own analysis had drifted toward checking
"was the AI Admiral" when the real question was always "what did the USER do, and does Legend
reflect it." See §0.12 for what came directly out of correcting this.

### 0.12 — What changed in v1.65-S76 (a real cross-tier NaN bug, plus a Legend refinement from
four combat logs of the user's own play)

**Source:** user-submitted combat log, `combat_log_2026-09-04-11-25-38.txt` (v1.64-S75) — USS
Constitution vs. IKS Devisor (D-7 M (IX)), shared as a positive example ("Solid narrative! Well
done!") but containing a real, visible bug: `AI allocated: Move 19→6pts, Shields NaN→NaNpts,
Weapons NaN`, and later in the same log, `Move NaN→NaNpts, Shields NaN→NaNpts, Weapons NaN` —
even the AI's own move points went NaN in the third power allocation.

**Root cause, traced to actual code, not inferred from symptoms:** `buildWeapon()` only ever
sets `.maxPower` on beam-type weapons — by design, since missiles and plasma torpedoes arm for
a fixed cost (`.armCost`) rather than drawing a variable amount of power the way a beam does. On
a missile-type weapon object, `.maxPower` is simply `undefined`, always, on purpose. **Three
separate AI difficulty branches — Cadet (`D===1`), Admiral (`D===5`, introduced by this
project's own v1.58-S69 fix), and Legend (`D===6`) — were all summing `w.maxPower` directly
across a ship's full weapons array** to compute how much power its weapons could collectively
use. The Klingon D-7 M (IX) in this log carries 3× `KD-8` (beam, `maxPower:7`) and 2× `KP-3`
(missile, `armCost:2`, no `.maxPower` at all) — the instant the reduce hit a `KP-3`,
`undefined + number` produced `NaN`, and once `NaN` entered that running sum it poisoned
everything computed from it afterward: weapon power, then shields (computed as
`tot-move-weapPwr`), and in a later turn of the same log, even move itself once a different
code path referenced the same poisoned value.

**Fix:** added one shared `weaponPowerCap(w)` helper, placed directly after `buildWeapon()`
since it's the natural counterpart to the asymmetric field-setting that caused this — returns
`w.maxPower||0` for beams, `w.armCost||0` for missile/plasma. All three call sites (search
`weaponPowerCap` — there should be exactly three, one each in Cadet/Admiral/Legend) now go
through it instead of touching `w.maxPower` raw. **Verified with a standalone Node
simulation of the exact D-7 M(IX) loadout from the log**: old pattern reproduces `NaN` exactly
as seen; new pattern correctly returns `25` (3×7 beam + 2×2 missile). Not just read the fix and
assumed it worked.

**Separately, a genuine Legend refinement, not a bug fix:** the user's actual request behind
sharing these logs was to have Legend (`D===6`) learn from the user's own demonstrated tactics,
independent of whatever difficulty a given log's AI opponent happened to be playing at (see the
correction note above §0.12 — this session had been checking the wrong thing for a few turns).
Across **four** combat logs now (spanning 2026-09-02 through 2026-09-04), the user's own
turn-by-turn power commitments show a clear, consistent pattern: **43-88% of total power to
Move on every turn except one deliberate all-in weapons turn** (12% move, when a kill was
already within clear reach). The mechanical reason this matters: Move determines Tactical
Advantage (who moves last, reactively, versus who's forced to expose their position first) —
and the enemy AI across these same logs converts to a flat, unchanging number of move points
every turn (always 2, or always 4 against a bigger ship), regardless of difficulty, making it
trivially beatable for initiative by anyone who invests meaningfully more. Legend's own
"aggressive closer, out of range" pattern (`Pattern 3/4` in the code comments) was already
tactical-advantage-aware in principle — `move=Math.floor(tot*0.45)` — just tuned low relative
to what four logs' worth of the user's actual play now shows. **Bumped to `0.55`**, landing in
the middle of the observed 43-88% range rather than jumping to the high end, since four games
is still a fairly small sample and Legend still needs enough left over for weapons/shields to
remain a credible threat, not just an evasive one. The other three Legend patterns (hunting a
cloaked target, repositioning under cloak, point-blank strike) were left untouched — this data
doesn't speak to those situations at all, and touching them on the strength of unrelated
evidence would be exactly the kind of overreach this project has tried to avoid elsewhere.

**Explicitly not yet done, and worth deciding on deliberately rather than assuming:** the user
also asked, in the same message, whether this kind of lesson should extend to *all* difficulty
settings, not just Legend. That's a real, bigger design question — every other tier's move
allocation is *also* a small fixed value or a low fixed percentage that would lose the same
tactical-advantage battle against play like this, but making every tier equally competitive for
initiative would flatten the intended difficulty curve (Cadet is supposed to be beatable; Legend
is supposed to be the one that plays like the user). This needs its own explicit design pass —
how much of a bump each tier gets, if any, to preserve a meaningful gradient — not a blanket
copy of Legend's new ratio onto Cadet/Ensign/Lt.Cmdr/Captain/Admiral. Flagged here rather than
guessed at.

### 0.13 — What changed in v1.66-S77 (USS Excelsior: repaired existing art, added a viewscreen
for the first time)

**Two real, independent problems reported by the user, from actually playing against this
ship**, plus a factual claim that needed checking rather than assuming:

**Problem 1 — genuine clipping on the port saucer edge of the existing `SHIP_SPRITES.Excelsior`
sprite**, predating this session (the art was already live before this conversation started).
Confirmed directly by decoding and viewing it: the starboard side showed a complete circular
arc, the port side was cut flat. **Fix:** found the ship's true vertical symmetry axis from the
nacelle pylons specifically (x=126, consistently across several rows), not assumed from the
256px canvas center (x=128) or from the ship's own bounding box (which was itself skewed by
the missing content on one side) — then mirrored the confirmed-good starboard half across that
axis onto the port side. This is a repair technique specific to genuinely bilaterally-symmetric
hull sections (a saucer, unlike the Klingon wingtip situation in §0.9, where the source art
itself turned out to be intentionally/accidentally asymmetric) — mirroring is only valid when
the missing side is known to be a defect, not a real design difference.

**Problem 2 — no `FRONT_VIEW_ART.Excelsior` entry existed at all.** Confirmed by direct search
before doing anything else (not assumed from the reported symptom alone) — this ship had never
had real viewscreen art, only the procedural fallback. User supplied a clean front-view image;
processed with the standard flood-fill transparency pipeline and added as a new entry. Checked
for left/right symmetry before accepting it (habit carried over from the Klingon work) —
confirmed clean, no repair needed this time.

**The claim that needed checking: the user believed an `Excelsior_integration.js`-style
reserve file already existed ("saved for later") with additional angles.** Searched the
project's stored files specifically for this before responding — no such file exists anywhere
this session can find. HANDOVER's own §4 explicitly lists every reserve-art bundle that does
exist (`Reliant`, `D10`, `Chandley`, `D7`, `D7RSM`, `WingedDefender`, `LoknarClass`), and
Excelsior has never been among them. Told the user this directly rather than either assuming
the file existed somewhere unseen or silently proceeding as if it didn't matter. **If a
different session or a later memory turns up an actual Excelsior reserve file, that would
contradict this finding and should take precedence** — this is a search-based negative result,
not a certainty, and this session has no visibility into any other conversation thread.

**A third request from the same message was NOT done, and needs the user's direction, not a
guess:** replacing "the procedurally generated image ... seen in the damage control section."
Investigated `dmgDrawShip()` before touching anything and found this view does **not** use
`SHIP_SPRITES` or any per-ship image at all — it calls one of exactly three shared,
per-*faction* procedural line-drawing functions (`drawFedShip`/`drawRomShip`/`drawKliShip`),
the same generic silhouette for every Federation ship regardless of class. Shield-face labels
and damage annotations are positioned using offsets (`SR`, `nacX`, `sY`, etc.) computed
against that generic silhouette's assumed proportions. **Naively swapping in real Excelsior art
here would either require it to replace the generic silhouette for every other Federation ship
too (Constitution, Enterprise, Reliant, Loknar, Chandley — all sharing `drawFedShip`), which
almost certainly isn't wanted, or would require building an entirely new per-ship image path
for this view plus re-deriving every label's position against each new image's actual
proportions rather than the procedural silhouette's.** This is meaningfully new engineering
work, not a sprite swap, and shouldn't be started on assumption. Whoever picks this up needs
the user's explicit call: keep the damage view procedural/generic for every ship (arguably
intentional — it reads as a FASA-style schematic, not a photo), or invest in per-ship damage
art with its own label-alignment system.

### 0.14 — What changed in v1.67-S78 (damage-control silhouettes made swappable — the simpler
alternative to §0.13's full parts/attachment system, chosen deliberately)

**Direct follow-up to the open question at the end of §0.13.** The user asked, correctly, for
the cheaper option: don't build a modular parts/attachment system yet (confirmed as future
work, logged separately — see the backlog item below) — just make the damage-control
silhouette swappable for real art on a per-ship basis, reusing the existing generic drawing as
the fallback for every ship without one.

**Why this really is the cheaper option, confirmed by reading `dmgDrawShip()` in full, not
assumed:** the shield-face labels, superstructure box track, and status text are ALL positioned
using a small set of shared constants (`SR`, `sY`, `nacX` — saucer radius, saucer height,
nacelle spread) computed once at the top of the function. None of that overlay code cares how
the silhouette underneath it was actually drawn. So the entire change is: add a lookup
(`DMG_VIEW_ART`, structured like `FRONT_VIEW_ART`) keyed by `spriteKey`; before calling
`drawFedShip`/`drawRomShip`/`drawKliShip`, check whether that ship has a real-art entry, and if
so, fit that image into the same envelope the procedural silhouette occupies instead. Every
ship without an entry falls through to the exact same procedural call as before — zero
regression risk.

**What was actually shipped this build:** `DMG_VIEW_ART` (empty), a small `getDmgImg()` image-
cache helper (lazy-loads and caches an `Image` object per key, since a data-URI image needs a
tick to report `.complete` — falls back to procedural on the rare first frame if it hasn't
loaded yet, not worth engineering around for something this fast), and the actual fit-to-
envelope math in `dmgDrawShip()` (a real image is fit into `shipW×(shipH+4)` units, preserving
its own aspect ratio, vertically offset by `4*U` to match the same forward/aft asymmetry the
procedural ships already have — verified with real numbers before shipping: for a ship
image with roughly a 1:2.5 aspect ratio, the fitted top/bottom edges land within a few units of
where the `FWD`/`AFT` label formulas already assume the ship's extent to be, without needing
any further tuning). A damaged ship gets a semi-transparent orange tint applied with
`source-atop` compositing, so it still reads as "hurt" without needing separate damaged-state
art. **This entire build shipped with `DMG_VIEW_ART` deliberately empty** — the infrastructure
was correct and complete, but no ship actually had real art in this view yet. See §0.15 for why
that distinction turned out to matter.

**Deliberately NOT done, and shouldn't be assumed later:** this is not the modular parts system
described in §0.13 (saucer, nacelles, pylons, etc. as independently placeable pieces with their
own transform). That remains real, unscoped future work — see the backlog entry. This build
only swaps the whole silhouette image as a single unit.

### 0.15 — What changed in v1.68-S79 (the Excelsior art promised in v1.67-S78 actually embedded)

**A real gap, worth being honest about rather than glossing over:** v1.67-S78's own changelog
said "starting with USS Excelsior," but `DMG_VIEW_ART` shipped empty (see §0.14's closing
note) — the infrastructure was genuinely finished and correct, but the specific example that
motivated it hadn't actually been wired in yet. This build closes that gap: `DMG_VIEW_ART.
Excelsior` is now populated.

**Source, and why it isn't just a copy of the tactical sprite:** reprocessed fresh from the
user's original high-resolution upload (`1788556524616_image.png`, the same top-down reference
used for the §0.13 tactical-sprite repair), not the already-shrunk 256×256 tactical sprite.
The damage-control display renders considerably larger than the tactical map icon, and reusing
the small sprite would have looked visibly soft at that size. Verified by decoding the embedded
image straight out of the saved game file, not just trusting the working PNG before insertion.

**Current state, precisely:** Excelsior is the only ship with real art in the damage-control
view. Every other ship (Constitution, Enterprise, Reliant, Loknar, Chandley, and all
Klingon/Romulan hulls) still uses the procedural `drawFedShip`/`drawRomShip`/`drawKliShip`
exactly as before — this was never a regression risk given how `DMG_VIEW_ART` is structured
(see §0.14), and remains true here. Adding another ship to this view going forward is just
another `DMG_VIEW_ART` entry, following the same recipe: source the highest-resolution art

bow-up, no fixed canvas size needed since `dmgDrawShip()` fits by aspect ratio.

### 0.16 — What changed in v1.69-S80 (a real, significant bug: terrain-based to-hit penalties
were purely cosmetic everywhere — asteroid cover, nebula sensor degradation, both directions)

**Source:** user-submitted combat log where the player lost against an Excelsior while
deliberately positioned in an asteroid field for cover — and got no apparent benefit from it.
The user's exact words, worth keeping: *"I was clearly IN among the asteroids. I should have
gotten the defense bonus for 'hiding.'"*

**This turned out to be a much bigger finding than "the AI doesn't check terrain."** Grepped
this entire file for every place a to-hit roll is actually computed and adjusted, looking for
any mechanism that modifies the chart's success band for terrain. Found exactly one real
to-hit modifier anywhere in the codebase: the existing cloak-detection penalty in
`resolveShipFiring()` (`effMax=maxR-(fireGate.penalty||0)`). **The asteroid-cover message
("+1 cover vs beam fire") and the nebula message ("+1 to required roll") were logged as
warnings in the player's own `fireWeapon()`, every single game, and never once actually
changed `maxR`, `effMax`, or the hit/miss outcome.** They read exactly like real mechanical
effects — specific numbers, specific rule language pulled from the `HOUSE_RULES`/legend
descriptions — while doing nothing. **Worse still: `resolveShipFiring()` (the AI's shared
firing function, used for every enemy shot in the game) had no terrain awareness of any
kind, not even the cosmetic message.** Terrain-based combat effects only existed, in name
only, on the player's own outgoing fire. The player could never have gotten a defensive
cover benefit from hiding in an asteroid field, regardless of position, because nothing
on the incoming-fire side ever looked at terrain at all.

**Fix:** added one shared `terrainToHitPenalty(shooterCol, shooterRow, targetCol, targetRow,
weaponType)` helper, placed directly after `canFireOnTarget()` since both govern to-hit
conditions. Returns a penalty to subtract from the chart's upper bound, the same mechanism
the cloak penalty already used — asteroid cover applies +1 only when the *target* is in
an asteroid hex and the firing weapon is a **beam** (matching the FASA rule text on the
`HOUSE_RULES`/legend entry exactly — torpedoes and plasma are unaffected by asteroid
cover), nebula applies +1 whenever *either* the shooter or the target is in a nebula hex,
regardless of weapon type, and these stack if both conditions are true. Wired into **both**
firing paths: the player's `fireWeapon()` (already had the log messages — now they're real)
and `resolveShipFiring()` (had neither the message nor the effect — now has both, added
alongside the existing `fireGate.penalty` cloak logic rather than as separate machinery).

**Verified with a standalone Node simulation before shipping, not just a read-through**:
confirmed beam-vs-asteroid triggers the penalty and missile-vs-asteroid does not (matching
the FASA text precisely), confirmed nebula penalties stack correctly and apply regardless
of weapon type, and — most importantly — replayed the exact numbers from the user's own
combat log (`FH-11 Bank 1: Chart Y Range 5 → need 1-6, rolled 1 — HIT!`) with the target
placed in an asteroid hex: the fixed code correctly drops the needed range to `1-5`, meaning
a roll of 6 that would have hit before the fix now correctly misses.

**Not touched, and a deliberate scope decision, not an oversight:** `weaponHitOutlook()`
(the pre-fire hit-chance estimate shown in the Power Allocation tab) and the AI's
fire/no-fire decision heuristics (`D===4`/`D===5`'s `>30%` gate, `D===6`'s always-fire logic)
still don't factor in terrain. Both are already explicitly documented as *estimates* that
don't account for everything that can change before the actual shot (movement happens after
power allocation, for instance) — adding terrain awareness there would improve accuracy
slightly but isn't part of this bug, which was specifically about the real dice roll never
reflecting terrain at all. Worth doing later if the AI's fire/hold-fire decisions start
looking odd around terrain specifically, but not bundled into this fix.
